newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean hostage report denied, exposes raw nerves.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean hostage report denied, exposes raw nerves.

text.p: The South Korean military denied a report on Wednesday that two South Koreans had been taken hostage by North Korean agents on the loose since they landed by submarine last month.
State-run Korea Broadcasting System triggered alarm by reporting that hostages were being held in a mountainous east coast area where a submarine delivered 26 North Korean agents last month.
It said the two had been picking mushrooms. A stand-off with South Korean troops ensued, it said.
"The story was wrong," said Major Kim Myong-shik, a Defence Ministry official based in the east coast city of Kangnung.
Two villagers were missing after last being spotted picking mushrooms on Tuesday, but there was no evidence they had been grabbed by North Koreans, said Kim.
State radio later reported the army was still combing the area around Mt Odae to find the missing villagers and put to rest lingering hostage fears.
After the hostage report surfaced the army "rapidly searched this area and confirmed the report was groundless", it said.

The episode exposed frayed nerves following a series of angry and potentially dangerous threats exchanged between Seoul and Pyongyang over the submarine incident and a charge of espionage by communist North Korea on Sunday.
North Korea has threatened "merciless retaliation" for the deaths of 22 of its soldiers killed by South Korean troops or found shot dead, vowing "blood should be paid for blood".
One of the North Koreans was captured while Seoul has wound down the hunt for the remaining three.
Pyongyang has demanded Seoul return the vessel along with the survivors and bodies of the dead crew.

Seoul has warned the North to stop its threats, saying any provocation will meet "stern punishment", while bolstering security at airports, ports, diplomatic missions and five west coast islands seen most vulnerable to any northern attack.

Pyongyang's charge on Sunday that it had nabbed a U.S. citizen spying for Seoul added more fuel to the fire. Seoul called the charge fabricated and said the man was a 22-year missionary based in northeast China.
A fragile ceasefire has kept the peace on the peninsula since the 1950-53 Korean War.
